🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Note: This design is heavily inspired from the DDP comm hook design proposed by @pritamdamania87 : #39272.
Implement an interface to register communication hooks to FSDP, similar to the DDP interface register_comm_hook: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/nn/parallel/distributed.py#L1348.
In the first implementation, the hook is only expected to work for the NO_SHARD (DDP) use case and can throw errors if the sharding strategy is anything else. However, we are designing it to be easily extensible to the generalized sharded case.
The hook should have the following interface:
def register_comm_hook(state: object, hook: Callable[torch.Tensor] -> None)
In particular, state is any object that the user might want to use to hold communication specific state (such as peers to communicate with in GossipGrad), and hook is the main communication hook implemented by the user.
The hook will be a function that takes in a python tensor (gradient that needs to be communicated across ranks), performs any communication, and returns nothing. Note that we don’t have to return a future here as this hook is already run on a separate stream so communication / computation is already overlapped.
When FSDP is ready to communicate a gradient, instead of call to dist.all_reduce (or _reduce_scatter in the future), we should invoke this hook and pass in the state and gradient tensor. We should also take care to not perform gradient pre-and post division in this case, as any division will be expected to be done by user algorithm.
Important detail: FSDP wrapping strategy can result in many (nested) FSDP instances in a single module hierarchy. Theoretically, these can all have different communication algorithms. Although, we will for now only allow one hook across the module hierarchy and share the same hook across all FSDP instances.
Overall, the flow with the hook will look as follows:
model = FSDP(model, auto_wrap=...)
model.register_comm_hook(state, hook) # shared across all FSDP submodules

def register_comm_hook(state, hook):
    self.hook = hook
    self.state = state
    # share hook and state with all submodules

// during communication
def _post_backward_hook(self):
    ...
    if hook:
        hook(grad, process group)
    else:
        dist.all_reduce(grad)


Note that the way that this hook is designed it is extensible to sharded gradients without any code changes - grad simply becomes a sharded gradient instead of a full gradient, and the user algorithm would need to be aware of this.
Please see #39272 for additional examples of gradient compression psuedocode algorithms.

Part of my model is being converted to float16 by autocast but another part is not.

        with torch.cuda.amp.autocast():

My model consists of an encoder, a quantizer, and a decoder.  The model is defined as
from vector_quantize_pytorch import ResidualVQ

class SoundStreamXL(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_io_channels, n_feature_channels, latent_dim, n_quantizers=8, codebook_size=1024):
        super().__init__()

        self.encoder = SoundStreamXLEncoder(n_io_channels=n_io_channels, n_channels=n_feature_channels, latent_dim=latent_dim)  
        self.decoder = SoundStreamXLDecoder(n_io_channels=n_io_channels, n_channels=n_feature_channels, latent_dim=latent_dim)

        self.quantizer = ResidualVQ(   # THIS ONE IS WHERE THE AUTOCAST FAILURE OCCURS
            num_quantizers=n_quantizers, 
            dim=latent_dim, 
            codebook_size=codebook_size,
            kmeans_init=True, 
            kmeans_iters=100, 
            threshold_ema_dead_code=2,

embed.dtype =  torch.float32

Currently derivatives.yaml codegens one derivative formula that gets registered for all autograd dispatch keys.  There are some functions like reshape_alias defined below.
- name: _reshape_alias(Tensor(a) self, int[] size, int[] stride) -> Tensor(a)
  self: grad.reshape(self.sizes())

One could define the function in: torch/csrc/autograd/VariableTypeManual.cpp and register it with:
TORCH_LIBRARY_IMPL(aten, Autograd*****, m)
Goal
The goal of this issue would be to define an extended schema to derivatives.yaml in order for multiple derivative implementations to be registered to different autograd dispatch keys.

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
primTorch's executor prototype currently uses torch.fx.experimental.proxy_tensor.make_fx function for creating an FX graph of operations. Currently make_fx supports only positional arguments and we need to expand the support to default positional and keyword-only arguments.
In [1]: import torch

In [2]: from torch.fx.experimental.proxy_tensor import make_fx

In [3]: def foo(a, b, alpha=1.0):
   ...:     return torch.add(a, b, alpha=alpha)
   ...:

In [4]: alpha = 0.5

In [5]: a = torch.randn(2, 2)

In [6]: b = torch.randn(2, 2)
Here are a few cases that should work:
# case 1
make_fx(foo)(a, b) # raises RuntimeError: Tracing expected 3 arguments but got 2 concrete arguments

# case 2
make_fx(foo)(a, b, alpha=alpha) # TypeError: wrapped() got an unexpected keyword argument 'alpha'

# case 3
make_fx(foo)(a, b, alpha)(a, b, alpha=alpha) # TypeError: forward() got an unexpected keyword argument 'alpha'

# case 4

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Numpy seems to support arithmetic operations on boolean arrays.
For instance one could do the following on numpy.
x = np.array([True, False, True])
x.mean()
0.6666666666666666

But on pytorch this is not supported yet.
x = torch.tensor([True, False, True])
x.mean()

RuntimeError                              Traceback (most recent call last)

      1 x = torch.tensor([True, False, True])
----> 2 x.mean()

RuntimeError: mean(): input dtype should be either floating point or complex dtypes. Got Bool instead.

Alternatives
But it seems that in pytorch the following operations are supported on bool Tensors.
x = torch.tensor([True, False, True])
x.sum().div(len(x))
tensor(0.6667)

These operations mean(x) = x.sum().div(len(x)) in principle are equivalent but the difference between them is a type cast I believe?
I think what pytorch does is converting the tensor x into floating point via the operation x.sum() and from there you are simply dividing 2 floating point numbers.
The question is what is mean doing internally, haven't check the code to see how is implemented but my guess is that it first checks the type of tensor x and if not in float or complex reject doing any operation, that's my best guess so far?

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
One of the most important options in profiler is record_shapes. It records the shape and dtype of inputs. This information is essential to for analyzing traces as without it there is no way to asses if an op has reasonable performance. However there are several things that we do not collect:

The identities of Tensors. Without this it is not possible to do data flow analysis.
The strides and layout of Tensors. Highly strided Tensors suffer from pathalogical memory/cache behavior and often kernes are not well optimized for these cased. Without strides two ops may be identical to the profiler but have very different runtime characteristics.
Scalar values. We capture that an input is a Scalar, but not the value itself. These values often parameterize computation (dim, groups, etc.) so proper analysis requires these values. (And they're scalars, so they should be cheap to store.)
More exotic types like TensorList or NestedTensor are important performance abstractions, but not handled by the profiler.

For (1), we can access the TensorImpl* and StorageImpl* when we encounter a Tensor. For (2), we already have an efficient packed sizes and strides representation that we use inside TensorImpl so it's mostly a matter of interfacing that with the profiler. (3) should be quite straightforward.
The input capture machinery in profiler was designed for extensibility (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/csrc/profiler/collection.h#L172-L202) so hopefully it will just be a matter of working through each case. And of course if you think of other things that might be useful feel free to add them as well.

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
When training FSDP with mixed precision and fp16, we need to be aware of the reduced range and avoid over/underflow. If we sum all gradients for a large world size and then divide, this might overflow the fp16 range and cause issues, while if we divide first and then sum, we may risk underflow. One possible solution is to divide by sqrt(N), run allreduce, and then divide the result again by sqrt(N) which is equivalent to a N = world size divide. As a result, allreduce only increases the magnitude by sqrt(N=world size), which is less likely to cause overflow.

The feature
Like Python List's add operator, + can be used to:

concatenate two torch.nn.Sequential into 1

The following Python code illustrating the idea, and possibly the implementation
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import TypeVar


class Sequential(list):
    def __add__(self, other):
        if isinstance(other, __class__):
            return __class__([*self, *other])
        else:
            raise TypeError(f"unsupported operand type(s) for +: {type(self)} and {type(other)}")
        

@dataclass
class Module(object):
    name: str = ""
    
    
if __name__ == '__main__':

    c = Sequential([a, b])
